slides.title: Constructions In Euclidean Geometry
slides.notes: Open by framing this chapter as a construction engine rather than a catalog of formulas. The class has already seen conformal objects; here the goal is to ask geometric questions as incidence constraints, combine the constraints with joins and meets, and then inspect the algebraic result before drawing a classical object.

slides.title: Incidence Probes
slides.notes: Use the three probes to make incidence computational. A point on a sphere has zero power, a point on a plane has zero signed plane probe, and a candidate construction is accepted only when the residual is small. This slide should make clear that the algebra replaces branching folklore with measurable tests.

slides.title: Coincidence
slides.notes: Emphasize that two descriptions can represent the same geometric constraint even when their raw coordinates differ by scale or by the way they were assembled. Coincidence is therefore a projective question about the represented set, not a literal array comparison. This is a useful debugging habit for conformal code.

slides.title: Join Then Meet
slides.notes: Present join and meet as complementary construction verbs. A join records the simplest object supported by given samples, while a meet asks which object satisfies several constraints at once. The diagram deliberately shows both directions so students do not identify construction with only intersection or only fitting.

slides.title: Circle-Line Intersections
slides.notes: Walk through the three circle-line cases as one discriminant story. The same algebraic meet can produce two real points, one tangent point, or an imaginary pair. The implementation lesson is to classify the result after construction, because the limiting tangent case should not require a different geometric pipeline.

slides.title: Plunge
slides.notes: The plunge is the chapter's way of keeping failed-looking intersections meaningful. When real objects do not intersect, the algebra can still return the simplest object contained in the constraints, often with imaginary radius or imaginary point-pair data. That retained information is useful for visualization and numerical continuation.

slides.title: Tangents Without Differentiating
slides.notes: Stress that tangency is expressed by incidence plus a point contact, not by taking a derivative of a parameterization. At a point on a circle, the tangent line is perpendicular to the radius and remains inside the carrier plane. The finite-difference check is only a sanity test, not the definition.

slides.title: Factorizing Rounds
slides.notes: Explain that a round object carries two pieces of geometry: its flat carrier and its surrounding sphere. Their meet recovers the original circle in the ordinary real case. This factorization is powerful because it makes carrier tests and radius tests separate, inspectable, and reusable in later constructions.

slides.title: Sphere And Circle Constraints
slides.notes: Use the sphere-sphere and sphere-plane examples to separate constraint assembly from drawing. Two spheres determine a radical circle when the radius is real, a tangent point in the limiting case, and an imaginary circle when the constraints miss. The same classification language applies to circle constraints.

slides.title: Projection As Constraint Transfer
slides.notes: Projection is not merely dropping a shadow in a drawing. The algebra transfers a round or flat object onto a target carrier and then checks the result by measuring residuals against the carrier constraint. The point is to keep the projected object's defining equations visible after the visual operation.

slides.title: Contour Circle
slides.notes: The contour construction is a useful applied example because it combines a sphere, an eye point, and a tangent condition. Every contour point lies on the sphere and has a sight line orthogonal to the radius. The slide should connect this to graphics silhouettes without turning it into a rendering lesson.

slides.title: Affine Dual Spheres
slides.notes: Describe affine combinations as a warning that linear algebra on conformal points changes object type. Between two finite points the normalized combination decodes as a dual sphere whose center follows the Euclidean affine point and whose squared radius can become negative. This is a feature to inspect, not a paradox.

slides.title: Voronoi Cell
slides.notes: Connect the Voronoi application to incidence rather than to a special diagram algorithm. Each neighbor contributes a half-plane constraint, and the cell is the feasible polygon left after clipping. The conformal viewpoint is helpful because edges and vertices are still checked by the same plane and point residuals.

slides.title: Robust Case Policy
slides.notes: This slide is the practical engineering checkpoint. Near tangency, near concentric spheres, and nearly collinear samples should be classified with tolerances and residuals, not hidden inside ad hoc branches. Students should leave with a policy: construct algebraically, classify geometrically, and report the residual that justified the branch.

slides.title: Algebraic Checks
slides.notes: Close by turning every construction into a short test list. Nullness, distance recovery, sphere power, tangent orthogonality, carrier residuals, and affine decoding are not optional afterthoughts; they are the way a conformal construction proves it is the intended Euclidean construction rather than a plausible drawing.
